text: A healthcare startup wants to build a system that summarizes patient intake forms, flags potential drug interactions, and routes urgent cases to a human nurse. The team has only two months to deliver a working prototype and limited budget for custom infrastructure. Which architectural pattern best fits this initial phase?
options: A fully autonomous multi-agent system with five specialized agents that independently negotiate task ownership
A monolithic fine-tuned model trained from scratch on proprietary patient data
An augmented LLM pattern using a single Claude call enhanced with retrieval and a structured output schema, escalating to a human for urgent flags
A rule-based expert system with no LLM component to avoid hallucination risk entirely
correct_answer: An augmented LLM pattern using a single Claude call enhanced with retrieval and a structured output schema, escalating to a human for urgent flags
explanation: Given the tight timeline, limited budget, and need for human oversight on urgent cases, an augmented LLM pattern (a single model call enhanced with tools/retrieval and structured output, option C) is the simplest architecture that meets the requirement, with human-in-the-loop escalation for safety. A complex multi-agent system (A) adds unnecessary orchestration overhead and risk for an early prototype; fine-tuning from scratch (B) is costly and slow; a rule-based system without an LLM (D) would not meet the summarization requirement.

text: A team is designing a claims-processing solution. The workflow includes extracting data from documents, validating against business rules, calculating payouts, and generating a decision letter. Each step is deterministic enough to be scripted, with only the document extraction and letter drafting requiring language understanding. Which decomposition approach best aligns with engineering best practices and cost control?
options: Decompose into a fixed workflow where Claude is only invoked for extraction and drafting steps, with deterministic code handling validation and calculation
Use a single large agentic loop where Claude autonomously decides the order of all four steps on every request
Have Claude perform all four steps in one long completion to minimize the number of API calls
Build four independent agents that each call Claude to re-verify the entire workflow end-to-end
correct_answer: Decompose into a fixed workflow where Claude is only invoked for extraction and drafting steps, with deterministic code handling validation and calculation
explanation: Because validation and calculation are deterministic, they should be handled by conventional code rather than the model, reducing cost, latency, and risk of error. Claude should be reserved for the two steps that genuinely require language understanding (option A). A fully agentic loop (B), a single mega-completion (C), or redundant verification agents (D) waste tokens and introduce unnecessary non-determinism into steps that have clear, fixed logic.

text: A team must choose between Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku variants for a high-volume product-tagging pipeline that processes millions of short product descriptions daily with a strict latency budget of under 500ms per call. text: A legal document review assistant must consistently output structured JSON with specific fields (`contract_type`, `risk_level`, `key_clauses`) for downstream parsing. Occasionally the model produces explanatory prose around the JSON despite instructions to return only JSON. What is the most effective combination of techniques to improve reliability?
options: Increase the temperature to encourage more varied, creative completions
Remove the system prompt entirely to simplify the context
Provide a few-shot example of the exact desired JSON output format and use a strict schema/output format constraint (`output_config.format` or strict tool schema)
Switch to zero-shot prompting with no examples to reduce token usage

Raising temperature (A) increases variability, removing the system prompt (B) removes guardrails, and switching to zero-shot (D) removes the examples that anchor semantic expectations.

text: A customer-facing chatbot repeatedly sends an identical 6,000-token brand voice guide and a 2,000-token FAQ document as part of every request, with only the final user turn changing. The team wants to reduce both per-request cost and time-to-first-token without losing any of the static content. Which combination of techniques best achieves this?
options: Summarize the brand guide to 500 tokens, accepting some loss of detail
Move the static content into the user's turn so it appears closer to the question
Switch the entire static content into a fine-tuned model to avoid sending it at all, even though fine-tuning was not previously budgeted
Place the static content first in the prompt and enable prompt caching so the repeated prefix is reused across requests
correct_answer: Place the static content first in the prompt and enable prompt caching so the repeated prefix is reused across requests
explanation: Prompt caching reduces repeated cost and latency for static prefixes without requiring any loss of content, provided the stable content is ordered before the dynamic portion (option D). Summarizing (A) loses detail, repositioning content into the user turn without caching (B) doesn't reuse prefix computation, and unplanned fine-tuning (C) introduces unbudgeted cost and maintenance overhead.

text: An architecture team is deciding how a Claude-based agent should discover and use dozens of internal tools (inventory lookup, pricing, shipping, returns, loyalty points) without overwhelming the context window or confusing the model's tool-selection logic. Which strategy best balances capability with context efficiency?
options: Use a progressive discovery strategy where the agent first queries a lightweight tool index and retrieves detailed schemas only for tools relevant to the current task
Load full descriptions and schemas for all dozens of tools into every system prompt so the model always has complete visibility
Hard-code a single tool that performs all functions internally to eliminate tool selection entirely
Randomly sample a subset of tools for each request to reduce token count
correct_answer: Use a progressive discovery strategy where the agent first queries a lightweight tool index and retrieves detailed schemas only for tools relevant to the current task
explanation: Progressive discovery (option A) avoids monolithic context bloat by letting the agent retrieve only relevant tool details on demand, improving both token efficiency and tool-selection accuracy. Loading all tool schemas upfront (B) causes capability bloat and context strain; a single mega-tool (C) reduces flexibility and transparency; random sampling (D) risks omitting needed tools.

text: A financial services firm is integrating Claude with internal systems that hold account balances, transaction history, and the ability to initiate wire transfers. The architecture team is evaluating authentication design. Which approach best reduces the security gap between what the agent can access and what a given user session should be authorized to do?
options: Use a single service-level API key with full system privileges shared across all agent instances for simplicity
Propagate the authenticated end-user's identity and scoped permissions through to each tool call, so the agent can only act within that user's authorization boundary
Disable authentication for internal network traffic since the agent is not exposed externally
Require the agent to ask the user for their password directly within the conversation before each sensitive action
correct_answer: Propagate the authenticated end-user's identity and scoped permissions through to each tool call, so the agent can only act within that user's authorization boundary
explanation: Proper authorization design requires that the agent operate within the authenticated user's own permission scope rather than a broad shared credential (option B), preventing privilege escalation. A single shared full-privilege key (A) creates a major security gap, disabling authentication internally (C) ignores insider-threat and lateral-movement risk, and asking for passwords in conversation (D) is an anti-pattern that risks credential exposure.

text: A RAG-based internal knowledge assistant indexes long technical manuals (50-200 pages each) with highly structured sections, tables, and cross-references. Users frequently ask narrow factual questions that require precise paragraph-level answers. Which chunking strategy is most appropriate?
options: Chunk entire documents as single units regardless of length to preserve all context
Use fixed-size chunks of 100 tokens with no regard to section or heading boundaries
Use semantic/structural chunking aligned to section and subsection boundaries, sized to capture coherent units of meaning
Avoid chunking altogether and pass the full corpus into the context window on every query
correct_answer: Use semantic/structural chunking aligned to section and subsection boundaries, sized to capture coherent units of meaning
explanation: Retrieval strategies should match the data shape; structured technical manuals benefit from chunking that respects logical boundaries (sections, headings, option C) so retrieved chunks are coherent and precisely relevant to narrow factual queries. text: After deploying a new prompt version, a team notices increased hallucinations in production but cannot yet tell whether the cause is the new prompt, a model version change, or a data pipeline issue. What is the most rigorous way to isolate the cause before making further changes?
options: Immediately roll back all changes simultaneously without further investigation
Assume it is a model issue and file a support ticket without internal testing
Run a controlled A/B test comparing the new prompt against the previous version on the same model and data pipeline, changing only one variable at a time
Increase the temperature setting to see if that resolves the hallucinations

text: During discovery for a new Claude-based solution, a business stakeholder states the goal as 'make our support team faster' without specifying measurable targets. As the architect, what is the most effective next step?
options: Proceed directly to building a prototype based on your own assumptions about what 'faster' means
Facilitate a structured requirements session to define measurable success criteria, such as target reduction in average handle time or first-response SLA
Tell the stakeholder that vague requirements make the project infeasible and should be abandoned
Select the most advanced model available and assume it will satisfy any interpretation of 'faster'
correct_answer: Facilitate a structured requirements session to define measurable success criteria, such as target reduction in average handle time or first-response SLA
explanation: Structured discovery and requirement gathering (option B) is essential to translate vague business goals into measurable, actionable success criteria before design begins. Proceeding on assumptions (A) risks building the wrong solution, declaring the project infeasible (C) is an overreaction, and model selection (D) cannot substitute for clarified requirements.

text: An architect has recommended a RAG-based architecture over a fine-tuning approach for a client's knowledge-base assistant. The client's legal team pushes back, questioning why the architect didn't choose fine-tuning for 'better accuracy.' What is the most effective way to communicate this architectural trade-off?
options: Dismiss the legal team's concern as outside their expertise and proceed without explanation
Agree to switch to fine-tuning immediately without technical justification, to avoid conflict
Provide only the technical specification document with no plain-language summary

Explain the trade-offs in terms the stakeholder can evaluate: RAG allows easier updates to source content, better traceability of answers to source documents, and lower retraining cost, versus fine-tuning's higher maintenance burden for frequently changing content
correct_answer: Explain the trade-offs in terms the stakeholder can evaluate: RAG allows easier updates to source content, better traceability of answers to source documents, and lower retraining cost, versus fine-tuning's higher maintenance burden for frequently changing content
explanation: Effective stakeholder communication requires translating technical trade-offs (RAG vs. fine-tuning) into business-relevant terms the audience can evaluate, including maintainability, traceability, and cost (option D). Dismissing concerns (A) or capitulating without justification (B) undermines trust and sound architecture, and providing only a technical document (C) fails to meet the stakeholder where they are.

text: A solution has been handed off from the architecture team to the operations team after deployment. Three months later, the model's behavior has drifted in subtle ways that stakeholders are only now noticing. Which lifecycle practice would have most likely caught this earlier?
options: Establishing ongoing monitoring and a structured feedback loop between operations and the architecture team, including periodic review of evaluation metrics post-launch
Treating deployment as the final phase of the project with no further architect involvement
Relying exclusively on end-user complaints as the sole detection mechanism
Re-running the full discovery phase from scratch every time an issue is suspected
correct_answer: Establishing ongoing monitoring and a structured feedback loop between operations and the architecture team, including periodic review of evaluation metrics post-launch
explanation: Lifecycle management extends beyond handoff into monitoring and iteration phases; a structured feedback loop with regular metric review (option A) enables early detection of drift. Treating deployment as the end of involvement (B), relying only on reactive user complaints (C), or restarting discovery from scratch for every issue (D) are all inefficient and fail to support continuous monitoring.

text: A development team using Claude Code reports that engineers spend significant time manually re-explaining the codebase's architecture and conventions to the assistant in every new session. Which configuration change would most improve developer productivity?
options: Instruct engineers to paste the entire codebase into every conversation manually

Set up persistent project-level context or configuration files (such as `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/`) that Claude Code automatically references, so conventions and architecture are available without repeated manual explanation
Disable the AI tool and return to fully manual coding workflows
Require a senior engineer to approve every single line of AI-suggested code individually before any session begins
correct_answer: Set up persistent project-level context or configuration files (such as `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/`) that Claude Code automatically references, so conventions and architecture are available without repeated manual explanation
explanation: Configuring persistent project-level context (such as `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/` files that Claude Code automatically loads, option B) reduces repetitive setup overhead and directly improves developer workflow efficiency. Manually pasting the whole codebase each time (A) is inefficient and consumes excessive tokens, abandoning the tool (C) forfeits productivity gains, and requiring exhaustive line-by-line pre-approval before any session (D) is an excessive process bottleneck unrelated to the root cause.
